name: Chunking Strategies
question: Does each retrieved piece hold the whole answer?
summary: Splits parsed documents into the pieces that are embedded and retrieved. Size and boundaries decide whether a retrieved chunk contains the full answer: too small and a rule loses its exception, too large and the embedding blurs and the prompt fills with noise. Common strategies are fixed-size with overlap, recursive splitting by paragraph and sentence, structure-aware splitting by heading or clause, semantic splitting where the topic shifts, and small-to-big retrieval that searches small chunks but returns their parent section.
useCases: Long, structured documents: policies, contracts, manuals, regulations
Answers that depend on a condition or exception
Corpora where a few chunk types answer most questions

code.text: sections = clauses.split_text(policy_md)          # one piece per clause

steps.title: Split along the document’s own structure
steps.text: Policy wordings are written as sections and clauses. Split on those headings first, so a clause starts and ends where its author meant.

steps.title: Split long clauses recursively
steps.text: A clause longer than about 400 tokens is split on paragraphs, then lines, then sentences, never mid-word. Most clauses stay whole.

steps.title: Overlap the edges
steps.text: 50 tokens of overlap mean a sentence cut at a boundary appears in both neighbours, so “except after 36 months” is not orphaned.

steps.title: Prepend the section path
steps.text: “[Policy › Exclusions › 4.2]” goes at the top of the chunk. A question about exclusions now matches a chunk whose text never uses that word.

steps.title: Search small, return the clause
steps.text: The search matches small, precise chunks; the prompt receives the whole parent clause, deduplicated, so the rule and its exception arrive together.

steps.title: Measure each strategy
steps.text: Compare recall at 5 and tokens per answer on real questions. Any change of chunking means re-embedding the corpus, so decide on evidence.

practice.scenario: Pragati Insurance, a fictional insurer, answers agents' questions about its policy wordings. It splits each document by section and clause, then recursively to about 400 tokens with a 50-token overlap, prepends the section path to each chunk, and retrieves small chunks but sends the whole clause to the model, so rules arrive with their exceptions.

industries.use: Policy wordings, where exclusions and waiting periods sit inside clauses
Contracts split by clause and schedule
Documentation split by heading, with code blocks kept whole

practice.analogy: Cutting a newspaper into clippings. Cut along the articles and write the section name on each clipping, not every 10 centimetres straight across the page.

library.name: LangChain text splitters
library.what: Recursive, token-aware and Markdown-header splitters; the most common starting point for chunking.

practice.note: Chunk sizes here are in tokens of the cl100k_base encoding; match the tokenizer of your embedding model where it matters.

samples.code:
from langchain_text_splitters import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

policy_md = open("health_policy.md").read()
headers = [("#", "doc"), ("##", "section"), ("###", "clause")]
sections = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(headers_to_split_on=headers).split_text(policy_md)

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_tiktoken_encoder(
    encoding_name="cl100k_base", chunk_size=400, chunk_overlap=50)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(sections)

for c in chunks:
    path = " > ".join(v for k, v in c.metadata.items() if k in ("doc", "section", "clause"))
    c.page_content = f"[{path}]\n{c.page_content}"
    c.metadata["parent"] = path

print(len(chunks), "chunks")
print(chunks[0].page_content[:200])

numericDrill.question: A corpus of 900,000 tokens is chunked at 300 tokens with no overlap. How many chunks, in thousands?
numericDrill.answer: 900,000 ÷ 300 = 3,000 chunks, or 3 thousand. With 20% overlap it would be about 3,600.

interview.question: How do you choose chunk size?
interview.answer: Start from the document structure and a few hundred tokens, then measure recall and tokens per answer on real questions. Small chunks match precise facts; larger ones keep conditions together. Small-to-big retrieval gets both: search small, return the parent section.

interview.question: What is contextual chunking?
interview.answer: Adding context to each chunk before embedding: at minimum the title and section path, or an LLM-written sentence situating the chunk in its document. It helps chunks match questions phrased in the document's own terms, at a one-off ingestion cost.

mistakes.mistake: Picking a chunk size once and never measuring it
mistakes.fix: Compare strategies on recall and tokens with real questions

mistakes.mistake: Cutting fixed-size chunks through clauses and tables
mistakes.fix: Split along headings, clauses and rows

quiz.question: A clause says “pre-existing diseases are excluded” and, 700 tokens later, “except after 36 months”. With 400-token fixed chunks, what happens?
options: Both sentences are always retrieved together
The exception may be in another chunk and missed
quiz.explanation: Fixed cuts can separate a rule from its exception.

quiz.question: What does a recursive character splitter do?
options: Splits at a fixed character count
Tries paragraphs, then lines, then sentences, then words, until pieces fit
quiz.explanation: It uses the largest natural separator that keeps pieces under the size.

quiz.question: A 1.2 million-token corpus is chunked at 400 tokens with 15% overlap. About how many chunks?
Why prepend “[Policy › Exclusions › 4.2]” to a chunk?
options: It is required by vector databases
The section path becomes part of the embedded text, so section-level questions match
quiz.explanation: Chunks often never repeat their section name; the path supplies it.

quiz.question: What is small-to-big retrieval?
options: Searching small chunks but sending their parent section to the model
Using a small model then a big one

quiz.question: Which are symptoms of chunks that are too large? Select all that apply.
options: Short facts rank lower because the embedding is diluted
quiz.explanation: Losing exceptions is a symptom of chunks that are too small or badly cut.

quiz.question: k = 5 chunks of 512 tokens reach the prompt. How many tokens is that?
You change chunk size from 512 to 256 tokens in production. What must happen?
options: Only new documents use the new size
quiz.explanation: Chunks are the embedded unit; changing them means re-embedding.

quiz.question: Semantic chunking splits where…
options: a fixed number of tokens is reached
the embedding similarity between neighbouring sentences drops
quiz.explanation: It places boundaries at topic shifts.

quiz.question: Which should never be split across chunks? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Rows, code blocks and sentences lose meaning when cut; long documents must be split.

quiz.question: Search returns three small chunks from the same clause. What should reach the prompt with small-to-big?
options: All three chunks and the clause
quiz.explanation: Deduplicate parents to keep prompts lean.

quiz.question: Which strategy suits a transcript with no headings?
quiz.explanation: Without structure to follow, split by meaning or by natural separators.

quiz.question: Recall is 90% at 256-token chunks with small-to-big, using 2,100 tokens per answer. At 512 tokens without it, recall is 88% for 2,560 tokens. Which is better?
options: 256 with small-to-big: higher recall, fewer tokens

quiz.question: Why add 10–15% overlap between chunks?
options: So sentences at a boundary appear whole in at least one chunk
quiz.explanation: Overlap costs a little storage and prevents orphaned sentences.

quiz.question: Product cards are 80 tokens each. How should they be chunked?
options: Keep each card whole as one chunk
quiz.explanation: Short, self-contained items are natural chunks.

quiz.question: What should you compare when choosing a chunking strategy? Select all that apply.
options: Recall at k on real questions
Number of chunks and re-embedding cost
The number of headings in the documents
quiz.explanation: Measure outcomes and costs; heading counts are an input, not a result.

quiz.question: Anthropic’s contextual retrieval adds what to each chunk before embedding?
options: A short model-written note situating the chunk in its document
quiz.explanation: The context note helps chunks match questions phrased in the document’s terms.

quiz.question: At 128-token chunks, questions about rules with exceptions get 40% recall. What is the best fix?
quiz.explanation: The whole clause must reach the model.

quiz.question: A 900,000-token corpus is chunked at 300 tokens with no overlap. How many chunks?
A guideline’s dosage table is split between two chunks mid-row. What should the chunker do?
options: Keep table rows intact, splitting only between rows
quiz.explanation: Split tables only at row boundaries and repeat the header.
